body.text: The ripple effects from years of rising living costs continue to make life challenging for Australians.
Hundreds of you have shared your experiences with the ABC.
Small businesses fear losing customers and staff. Home owners worry about paying bills and putting food on the table.
While Australia has so far avoided a technical recession, many of the warning signs associated with one are becoming harder to ignore.
The unemployment rate has climbed to 4.9 per cent, its highest level of the post-pandemic period, and a Roy Morgan poll shows consumer confidence is at its lowest in seven months.

Artificial Intelligence, offshoring, restructuring and slowing economic activity are why Bunnings, Canva, NAB, Bendigo Bank, ING and Qantas are just some of the major businesses that have cut thousands of jobs in recent months.
At the same time, living costs continue to rise faster than many household budgets can absorb.
But whether that amounts to a recession depends on how you define one.
Technical recession versus lived reality
A recession is usually described as a period when the economy stops growing and starts going backwards.

The most commonly used measure, known as a "technical recession", is two consecutive quarters of negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP), which is the value of all goods and services produced across the country.
When recessions happen, businesses tend to earn less, consumers cut back their spending and unemployment often rises as companies reduce staff or delay hiring them.
By that definition, Australia is not in a recession. In fact, the economy is still growing, albeit slowly.
GDP rose 0.4 per cent in the June quarter and was up 2.1 per cent over the year.
Oxford Economics director of global macro research, Ben May, said some of the conditions that had historically preceded recessions were visible today in economies around the world.
"These features are visible in elevated energy prices, rising bond yields, and the AI boom," Mr May said.
"Still, compared with the 1970s and 1980s, economies are better positioned to weather shocks.
"It would take a further escalation in these or a sharp reversal of the AI boom to push the world economy into recession; a possible but not inevitable outcome."
So, Australia is not in an official recession, but there are other measures in the economists' tool box.

For instance, years of rising prices, higher mortgage repayments and wages that have struggled to keep pace with household costs have created what economists often describe as a "per capita recession" or a decline in living standards despite continued economic growth.
But even here, there's a disparity between how Australians feel about the economy and what the numbers say.

Abhijit Surya, senior APAC economist at Capital Economics, said Australia had not yet entered a per capita recession, with official data showing real GDP per person fell slightly in the March quarter before edging higher in the June quarter.
"However, that's far from a stellar outcome," Mr Surya said.
"With the economy set to slow markedly, we wouldn't rule out the possibility that Australia enters a per capita recession over the next few quarters."
That disconnect has become a growing part of the national conversation.

Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock recently acknowledged that conditions were "going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer" following the central bank's decision to raise the cash rate to 4.85 per cent.
So while the economy may still be growing "on paper", around kitchen tables and business counters, many Australians tell a different story.
Every dollar counts
Albury resident Nicole Thurgate is feeling the economic pain at home.
"I feel like I'm in a recession and it definitely feels like we're going backwards," Ms Thurgate said.
"You just feel like it's never going to end. There's just so little hope."
The 57-year-old said it was around the time of the third interest rate rise of 2026 that the combined pressure of rising mortgage repayments and living costs became impossible to ignore.
Since then, she has cut back on almost every discretionary expense she can think of.

Her car is off the road because she cannot afford repairs, she has sold personal belongings including her mother's jewellery and a perfume collection, and has stopped buying takeaway food and red meat altogether.
"It's not just giving up luxuries here," she said.
"[It's] basic things, right down to the kind of tea bag I'm buying. It's become every cent.
"So when you read something that says people just need to give up luxuries, I don't have any more left."
After paying bills, Ms Thurgate said she was often left with just $50 to $60 a fortnight for groceries.
Adding to the pressure is growing concern about job security.
Ms Thurgate said hundreds of positions had been made redundant at her workplace in the past year, with more cuts flagged in recent meetings.
"I am terrified because, if that happened, I don't know what I would do," she said.
"While I do have fantastic experience, let's be realistic: When it comes to applying for jobs, 57-year-old women aren't that popular."
The spending decisions being made around kitchen tables are also affecting small businesses.
Andrew Bianco, who runs Ragtime Tavern in Preston, Victoria, said patrons were still coming through the door but spending less.
"The main thing we've noticed is that people will come in for the live music and only drink water," he said.
"They won't order anything."
Mr Bianco recalled a recent "strange" moment when a group shared just two drinks between them.
"I've never seen that before," he said.
While customers are tightening their budgets, the cost of running his business is moving in the opposite direction.
Faced with rising supplier, insurance and operating costs, the venue recently increased prices after holding off for as long as possible.
"We just had no choice because the current economic climate has become quite erratic," he said.
For Queensland mother-of-three Crissy McDonald, the squeeze is on everything, from grocery shopping to Christmas planning.
"It's as if we are in a recession but without that big, scary word,"
Ms McDonald said.
"Our mortgage repayments alone now are my husband's total income, and we are relying on savings to buy our groceries and pay our bills."
She said her husband's roofing business had also felt the effects of higher interest rates, with several customers cancelling work as rates had climbed.
"People don't seem to be spending. They're really tightening up their budgets," the 31-year-old said.
"My husband has even told his apprentice that he'll keep him on as long as he can, but there's no guarantee."
At home, the family has cut swimming lessons, stopped eating out and declined invitations to children's birthday parties to keep spending under control.
"I am stressed and so cautious about everything and counting every cent for groceries to stay on top of our budget, which doesn't go far with three children," she said.
"We save as much as we can on electricity, reduce our water usage and, for Christmas, our children won't be getting anything but a card and some chocolate in their stockings, which is horrible.
"You work hard, you do all the right things, but it just feels like everything costs more and more."
When pessimism becomes an economic risk
Economists say the challenge for policymakers is that pessimism itself can become an economic headwind.
Mr Surya said weaker confidence raised the risk of households pulling back spending, which in turn could slow economic activity further.
"As households become increasingly pessimistic about their budgets and living standards, they may feel compelled to tighten their belts further," he said.
Mr Surya said the path to a lower inflation economy was unlikely to be painless.
"Mortgagors will be particularly squeezed in the near term," he said.
"Even once inflation is tamed, there is a risk that consumer sentiment remains depressed for some time.
"Real wages have fallen considerably over the past few years, and it will take a long time for those losses to be recouped."
